implementation_notes: std::expected is the standard Either instance: expected<T, E> is the effect context, and_then takes a callable that returns another expected (bind), transform applies a plain function (map), and or_else/transform_error touch the error channel; the chain short-circuits on the first unexpected value. std::optional with its C++23 and_then/transform is the same structure for absence. Use the classic hand-rolled form only when the toolchain predates C++23 or a library such as Boost.Outcome is already in the stack.
pitfalls: Using transform with a callable that returns an expected nests expected<expected<T, E>, E>; bind steps require and_then and the compiler does not warn about the extra layer.
Unwrapping without has_value() throws bad_expected_access (or skips the check with operator*), so the effect must not be discarded mid-pipeline.
std::expected must not be instantiated with reference or function types, which rules out the naive 'expected<T&, E>' bind over borrowed values.

variants.name: Ranges view pipeline (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: For the list/stream instance a lazy view pipeline is the monadic chain: transform is map and piping through views::join flattens the ranges produced by each step, which is bind for ranges (C++23 adds join_with). Prefer it for multi-valued, pull-based pipelines over containers; combine it with std::expected only when a step has its own failure channel, since ranges model nondeterminism/iteration rather than absence.
pitfalls: Views are lazy and non-owning: a pipeline over a temporary (or over a lambda result that dangles) is undefined behaviour; keep the owning container alive.
join consumes the inner ranges: over an input range that yields ranges by value, elements are moved out, so a second pass sees empty sequences.

variants.name: C++20 coroutines as the IO monad
variants.idiom_name: co_await on a task/awaitable type (cppcoro, Boost.Asio awaitable)
variants.implementation_notes: For asynchronous I/O the coroutine machinery plays the IO monad's role: a coroutine body is a suspended computation value, co_await is the sequencing step that resumes it with the awaited result, and the awaitable's promise type decides propagation and scheduling. This is monadic composition without a Monad interface, which is why C++ code spells it with a library (cppcoro task<T>, Boost.Asio's awaitable) rather than a home-grown do-notation.
pitfalls: A coroutine frame is heap-allocated and owned by the awaitable's promise type; dropping a handle without resuming it silently cancels the computation.
Storing references into a coroutine frame across a suspension point dangles; keep awaited data owned or outlive the coroutine.
